correctness.rationale: For finite vertex-transitive graphs the three-round EF-game invariant is precisely which ordered-pair adjacency and four possible third-vertex extension types occur: its necessity follows from rank-three existential/nonexistential witness sentences, and sufficiency from a strategy that matches the first vertex by transitivity, the second by a pair profile, and the third by a matching extension type. For H(d,q), common neighbors of distance-1/2/3-or-more pairs are q−2/2/0; subtracting degree and the pair gives the exact exclusive and neither-neighbor counts. Elementary strictly increasing differences in d and q establish all positive-zero boundaries for every parameter, yielding eight pairwise different spectra and the sharp 27-vertex smallest Hamming representative of the generic class. Johnson distances give common neighbors n−2/4/0; direct inequalities ensure the two advertised Johnson spectra. A separately executed checker directly constructs and compares 116 finite graphs, but this finite evidence is not used to infer the unbounded theorem.

value.rationale: The current Johnson-model-theory literature explicitly motivates understanding Hamming first-order limit theories. This theorem gives the complete sharp rank-three answer for every finite Hamming graph, with eight qualitatively different parameter regimes, nontrivial thresholds d=3 versus 4 in the binary case and d=2 versus 3 in the nonbinary case, a 27-point optimal Hamming representative of the eventual rank-three theory, and a surprising cross-family equivalence to Johnson graph theories at the same depth. A complete natural bounded-depth classification is useful independently of the unresolved full first-order limit-theory problem, and these distinctions cannot be read from simple counts of vertices or edges alone.
